title: Rigveda 7.49: To the waters
source: Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 (undated (catalogued with Penn's 18th-19th c. Vedic manuscripts)), OPenn, Public Domain Mark + Aufrecht's accented text (GRETIL) + Griffith's English (VedaWeb)
description: Rigveda 7.49: To the waters: Sanskrit text and Griffith's English, each verse linked to the page of an undated Rigveda manuscript (Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41) that carries it.
introduction:
Rigveda 7.49 is a hymn of 4 verses addressed to the waters. It stands in book (maṇḍala) 7, the family book of Vasiṣṭha. The Rigveda is the oldest collection of Sanskrit hymns, composed in the second half of the second millennium BCE and handed down orally for many centuries before it was written down.

The manuscript shown is Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 (University of Pennsylvania), an undated paper manuscript of the padapāṭha (the word-by-word recitation text, in which every word is written separately and compounds are split) of the whole Ṛgveda in Devanāgarī, 884 leaves in fascicles, 7-9 lines to the page, accents in red; this hymn stands on fol. 525r. Each section below gives the verses that end on one page; the page boundaries were read on the images (the opening words of every page), not counted out. Where the manuscript is a padapāṭha (the word-by-word recitation text), the section shows Aufrecht's continuous (saṃhitā) text first and, as the edition text, the padapāṭha of the same verses, which is the form written on the page.
translator_notes: Sanskrit: Aufrecht's edition (1877) with the Vedic accents, as entered by van Nooten and Holland (GRETIL).

English: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda (1889-1892; 2nd ed. 1896-1897), from the VedaWeb digital text; OCR slips in that text were corrected against the printed 2nd edition (data/sources/rigveda/griffith_errata.json).
Padapāṭha (edition text): Sansknet e-text via GRETIL (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

translation.original_ref: RV 7.49.1-4 (aṣṭaka 5, adhyāya 4, varga 16); Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 fol. 525r
translation.original_text:
1sa̱mu̱drajye̍ṣṭhāḥ sali̱lasya̱ madhyā̍t punā̱nā ya̱nty ani̍viśamānāḥ | indro̱ yā va̱jrī vṛ̍ṣa̱bho ra̱rāda̱ tā āpo̍ de̱vīr i̱ha mām a̍vantu ||
2yā āpo̍ di̱vyā u̱ta vā̱ srava̍nti kha̱nitri̍mā u̱ta vā̱ yāḥ sva̍ya̱ṁjāḥ | sa̱mu̱drārthā̱ yāḥ śuca̍yaḥ pāva̱kās tā āpo̍ de̱vīr i̱ha mām a̍vantu ||
3yāsā̱ṁ rājā̱ varu̍ṇo̱ yāti̱ madhye̍ satyānṛ̱te a̍va̱paśya̱ñ janā̍nām | ma̱dhu̱ścuta̱ḥ śuca̍yo̱ yāḥ pā̍va̱kās tā āpo̍ de̱vīr i̱ha mām a̍vantu ||
4yāsu̱ rājā̱ varu̍ṇo̱ yāsu̱ somo̱ viśve̍ de̱vā yāsūrja̱m mada̍nti | vai̱śvā̱na̱ro yāsv a̱gniḥ pravi̍ṣṭa̱s tā āpo̍ de̱vīr i̱ha mām a̍vantu ||
translation.text:
1FORTH from the middle of the flood the Waters-their chief the Sea-flow cleansing, never sleeping. Indra, the Bull, the Thunderer, dug their channels: here let those Waters, Goddesses, protect me.
2Waters which come from heaven, or those that wander dug from the earth, or flowing free by nature, Bright, purifying, speeding to the Ocean, here let those Waters. Goddesses, protect me.
3Those amid whom goes Varuṇa the Sovran, he who discriminates men's truth and falsehood- Distilling meath, the bright, the purifying, here let those Waters, Goddesses, protect me.
4They from whom Varuṇa the King, and Soma, and all the Deities drink strength and vigour, They into whom Vaiṣvânara Agni entered, here let those Waters, Goddesses, protect Me.
translation.scan_note: Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41, fol. 525r (numbered 46r by the scribe) (OPenn image 525, lower leaf). Checked on the image: the Rigveda text on this page begins in RV 7.48.3 ‹te cit hi pūrvīḥ›. The next page with Rigveda text, fol. 525v (numbered 46v by the scribe), begins in RV 7.50.1 ‹-mitrāvaruṇā iha rakṣatam kulāyayat›. Verses 7.49.1-4 end on this page.
